title: Make a Permutation!
statementMd:
Ivan has an array consisting of $*n*$ elements. Each of the elements is an integer from $1$ to $*n*$.

Recently Ivan learned about permutations and their lexicographical order. Now he wants to change (replace) *minimum* number of elements in his array in such a way that his array becomes a *permutation* (i.e. each of the integers from $1$ to $*n*$ was encountered in his array exactly once). If there are multiple ways to do it he wants to find the *lexicographically minimal* permutation among them.

Thus minimizing the number of changes has the first priority, lexicographical minimizing has the second priority.

In order to determine which of the two permutations is lexicographically smaller, we compare their first elements. If they are equal — compare the second, and so on. If we have two permutations $*x*$ and $*y*$, then $*x*$ is lexicographically smaller if $*x*_{*i*} < *y*_{*i*}$, where $*i*$ is the first index in which the permutations $*x*$ and $*y*$ differ.

Determine the array Ivan will obtain after performing all the changes.

## Input

The first line contains an single integer $*n*$ ($2 ≤ *n* ≤ 200 000$) — the number of elements in Ivan's array.

The second line contains a sequence of integers $*a*_{1}, *a*_{2}, ..., *a*_{*n*}$ ($1 ≤ *a*_{*i*} ≤ *n*$) — the description of Ivan's array.

## Output

In the first line print $*q*$ — the minimum number of elements that need to be changed in Ivan's array in order to make his array a permutation. In the second line, print the *lexicographically minimal* permutation which can be obtained from array with $*q*$ changes.

## Note

In the first example Ivan needs to replace number three in position $1$ with number one, and number two in position $3$ with number four. Then he will get a permutation `[1, 2, 4, 3]` with only two changed numbers — this permutation is lexicographically minimal among all suitable.

In the second example Ivan does not need to change anything because his array already is a permutation.
statementZhMd:
Ivan 有一个包含 $*n*$ 个元素的数组。每个元素都是一个从 $1$ 到 $*n*$ 的整数。

最近，Ivan 学习了排列及其字典序。现在，他希望以*最少*的元素修改次数改变（替换）数组，使其成为一个*排列*（即 $1$ 到 $*n*$ 的每个整数都恰好在数组中出现一次）。如果有多种修改方式，他希望从中找到*字典序最小*的排列。

因此，最小化修改次数具有第一优先级，字典序最小化具有第二优先级。

为了确定两个排列中哪个字典序更小，我们比较它们的第一个元素。如果相等，则比较第二个元素，以此类推。对于两个排列 $*x*$ 和 $*y*$，如果 $*x*_{*i*} < *y*_{*i*}$，则称 $*x*$ 的字典序小于 $*y*$，其中 $*i*$ 是排列 $*x*$ 和 $*y*$ 首个不同的位置。

请确定 Ivan 完成所有修改后得到的数组。

## 输入格式

第一行包含一个整数 $*n*$（$2 ≤ *n* ≤ 200 000$）——Ivan 数组中的元素个数。

第二行包含一个整数序列 $*a*_{1}, *a*_{2}, ..., *a*_{*n*$}（$1 ≤ *a*_{*i*} ≤ *n*$）——Ivan 数组的描述。

## 输出格式

第一行输出 $*q*$——为了使 Ivan 的数组成为一个排列，至少需要修改的元素个数。第二行输出通过 $*q*$ 次修改可以从该数组得到的*字典序最小*排列。

## 说明

在第一个样例中，Ivan 需要将位置 $1$ 上的数字 $3$ 替换为数字 $1$，并将位置 $3$ 上的数字 $2$ 替换为数字 $4$。这样，他将得到排列 `[1, 2, 4, 3]`，只修改了两个数字；在所有符合条件的排列中，该排列的字典序最小。

在第二个样例中，Ivan 不需要进行任何修改，因为他的数组已经是一个排列。
